items.stem: A firm is productively efficient when it produces at the output where
options: average total cost is at its minimum
items.answer: average total cost is at its minimum
items.markingKey: Productive efficiency: lowest point of ATC (and for an economy, on the PPC).

items.stem: Explain why allocative efficiency requires price to equal marginal cost.
items.answer: Price measures the value consumers place on the last unit (marginal benefit) and MC the opportunity cost of producing it. If P > MC, society values extra units more than they cost, so output should rise; if P < MC, too much is produced. Only at P = MC is welfare maximised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: P = marginal benefit; 1 mark: MC = opportunity cost; 1 mark: P > MC under-production and vice versa [3]

items.stem: Explain why a monopolist is unlikely to be productively or allocatively efficient.
items.answer: A profit-maximising monopolist produces where MC = MR, which is below the output at minimum ATC and where P > MC, so it restricts output and charges a higher price.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MC = MR; 1 mark: P > MC (allocative inefficiency); 1 mark: not at min ATC [3]

items.stem: A firm producing cement has the following costs. Output (units): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; Total cost ($): 126, 150, 170, 194, 230, 286, 370, 490. At which output is the firm productively efficient?
items.answer: 5 units

items.stem: A firm producing bottled water has these costs. Output (units): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; Total cost ($): 139, 155, 174, 202, 245, 309, 400, 524. (a) Calculate average total cost at each output and identify the productively efficient output. (b) The market price is $91. Identify the allocatively efficient output and explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) ATC: 139, 77.5, 58, 50.5, 49, 51.5, 57.1, 65.5; productively efficient at 5 units (ATC $49). (b) 7 units, where MC = P = $91.
items.markingKey: (a) ATC = TC/Q [2]; min ATC at 5 [1]. (b) MC = ΔTC: 19, 16, 19, 28, 43, 64, 91, 124 [1]; P = MC at 7 units [1]; P = MC means marginal benefit = marginal cost [1].

items.stem: A firm producing restaurant meals has these costs. Output (units): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; Total cost ($): 121, 139, 160, 190, 235, 301, 394, 520. items.answer: (a) ATC: 121, 69.5, 53.3, 47.5, 47, 50.2, 56.3, 65; productively efficient at 5 units (ATC $47). (b) 7 units, where MC = P = $93.
items.markingKey: (a) ATC = TC/Q [2]; min ATC at 5 [1]. (b) MC = ΔTC: 21, 18, 21, 30, 45, 66, 93, 126 [1]; P = MC at 7 units [1]; P = MC means marginal benefit = marginal cost [1].

items.stem: The government of Umbria Nova is reviewing whether markets for laptops and for cement services are working efficiently. To what extent do you agree that a market economy will always allocate resources efficiently?
items.answer: Arguments for: Prices act as signals and incentives; competitive markets lead to P = MC. Arguments against / evaluation: Market failures: externalities, public goods, information failure, market power, immobility; efficiency is not equity. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.

items.stem: Allocative efficiency occurs where
options: average revenue equals average variable cost
marginal cost is at its minimum
items.answer: price equals marginal cost
items.markingKey: P = MC: the value consumers place on the last unit equals the cost of producing it.

items.stem: Distinguish between productive efficiency for a firm and for a whole economy.
items.answer: For a firm it means producing at the minimum point of its average cost curve; for an economy it means being on the PPC so no more of one good can be produced without producing less of another.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Keystone plc has cut its average cost of producing fresh fruit by adopting new machinery, but still produces less than the output at which average cost is lowest. Explain whether it is productively efficient.
items.answer: No: productive efficiency requires output at the minimum of the ATC curve using the least-cost method; producing below that output means ATC is still above its minimum.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: definition (min ATC); 1 mark: application [2]

items.stem: The government of Lunaria is reviewing whether markets for bottled water and for electricity supply services are working efficiently. Consider whether perfect competition is the most efficient market structure.
items.answer: Arguments for: In LR perfect competition P = MC = min ATC, so firms are productively and allocatively efficient; no X-inefficiency. Arguments against / evaluation: No funds for R&D so little dynamic efficiency; no economies of scale; assumptions unrealistic; natural monopoly may have lower costs; efficiency must be weighed against equity. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.

items.stem: Pareto optimality is a situation in which
options: total utility of each person is maximised
it is impossible to make one person better off without making someone else worse off
items.answer: it is impossible to make one person better off without making someone else worse off
items.markingKey: Pareto optimum: no further Pareto improvement is possible.

items.stem: Explain the conditions needed for an economy to achieve Pareto optimality.
items.answer: It must be productively efficient (on the PPC, firms at minimum cost) and allocatively efficient (P = MC in all markets), with no market failures.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: productive; 1 mark: allocative; 1 mark: P = MC everywhere/no market failure [3]

items.stem: Explain why a Pareto optimal allocation may still be considered unfair.
items.answer: Pareto optimality says nothing about distribution: an allocation where one person has almost everything can be Pareto optimal because any change would make them worse off.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: efficiency not equity; 1 mark: example [2]

items.stem: The table shows the utility of two people under five allocations of resources (utility values). P: Noah 34, Leila 51; Q: Noah 27, Leila 58; R: Noah 36, Leila 53; S: Noah 27, Leila 47; T: Noah 43, Leila 51. Starting from allocation P, identify which moves are Pareto improvements and explain.
items.answer: Pareto improvements: R, T. In these moves neither person is worse off and at least one is better off; the other moves make someone worse off.
items.markingKey: For each allocation compare both utilities with P [2]; correct list [1]; reason: no-one worse off, someone better off [1].

items.stem: The table shows the utility of two people under five allocations of resources (utility values). P: Amara 59, Omar 47; Q: Amara 59, Omar 55; R: Amara 61, Omar 52; S: Amara 74, Omar 42; T: Amara 57, Omar 41. Starting from allocation P, identify which moves are Pareto improvements and explain.
items.answer: Pareto improvements: Q, R. In these moves neither person is worse off and at least one is better off; the other moves make someone worse off.
items.markingKey: For each allocation compare both utilities with P [2]; correct list [1]; reason: no-one worse off, someone better off [1].

items.stem: A report on the economy of Gorvania claims that resources are allocated optimally. (a) Explain the difference between Pareto optimality and dynamic efficiency. (b) Discuss whether dynamic efficiency is more important than static efficiency for consumers in the long run.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Innovation lowers costs and creates new products; benefits compound over time; static gains are one-off. (b) Case for the view: Innovation lowers costs and creates new products; benefits compound over time; static gains are one-off. Case against / evaluation: Monopoly profits may not be reinvested; X-inefficiency; consumers pay higher prices now; competition can also drive innovation; depends on industry (pharmaceuticals vs retail). Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: A Pareto improvement is a change that
options: redistributes income from rich to poor
makes at least one person better off and nobody worse off
items.answer: makes at least one person better off and nobody worse off
items.markingKey: Pareto improvement: gains without losers.

items.stem: Explain how supernormal profit may lead to dynamic efficiency.
items.answer: Supernormal profit provides funds for research and development and the incentive of protected future profits, leading to new products and lower-cost processes over time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: funds R&D; 1 mark: incentive/outcome [2]

items.stem: Tidewater plc, a monopoly supplier of concert tickets in Halvoria, spent $12 million on research. Over 2 years its average cost fell from $50 to $30 per unit while output stayed at 5 million units a year. Calculate (a) the percentage fall in average cost and (b) the annual cost saving. (c) Explain whether this is evidence of dynamic efficiency.
items.answer: (a) 40% (b) $100 million a year (c) Yes: costs fell over time through innovation funded by profit; the research cost is recovered in about 0.1 years of savings, though consumers gain only if lower costs are passed on in price or quality.
items.markingKey: (a) (50 − 30)/50 × 100 = 40% [1]; (b) 20 × 5m = $100m [1]; (c) definition of dynamic efficiency applied [1] + evaluative point (pass-through to consumers / monopoly) [1].

items.stem: Market failure occurs when
options: the free market fails to allocate resources efficiently, so welfare is not maximised
the government intervenes in a market
items.answer: the free market fails to allocate resources efficiently, so welfare is not maximised
items.markingKey: Market failure: resource allocation is not allocatively (or productively) efficient.

items.stem: Explain why a public good such as street lighting would not be provided by a free market.
items.answer: Because it is non-excludable, consumers can free ride, so no firm can charge for it and make a profit; because it is non-rival, the marginal cost of an extra user is zero. The market is missing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: non-excludable → free riding; 1 mark: no profit → missing market; 1 mark: non-rival [3]

items.stem: Explain how monopoly power leads to market failure.
items.answer: A monopolist restricts output and raises price above MC, so P > MC (allocative inefficiency) and there is a deadweight welfare loss; it may also be X-inefficient.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: higher price/lower output; 1 mark: P > MC; 1 mark: deadweight loss [3]

items.stem: Unemployed coal miners in Lunaria cannot easily move to jobs in software development. Which type of market failure is illustrated?
items.answer: Factor immobility
items.markingKey: Factor immobility: the market outcome is not allocatively efficient for this reason.

items.stem: Smoke from a cement works in Nairobi damages crops on nearby farms. Which type of market failure is illustrated?
items.answer: Negative production externality
items.markingKey: Negative production externality: the market outcome is not allocatively efficient for this reason.

items.stem: In Calvania, private markets supply too little education and too many sugary drinks. (a) Explain how information failure leads to market failure. (b) Discuss whether information failure is the most important cause of market failure.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Asymmetric information, merit/demerit goods, adverse selection and moral hazard misallocate resources widely. (b) Case for the view: Asymmetric information, merit/demerit goods, adverse selection and moral hazard misallocate resources widely. Case against / evaluation: Externalities and market power may cause larger welfare losses; information can be improved cheaply; importance varies by market. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a merit good and a public good.
items.answer: A public good is non-rival and non-excludable and would not be provided at all by the market. A merit good is rival and excludable and is provided by the market, but in too small a quantity because its benefits are underestimated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition; 1 mark: not provided vs under-provided [3]

items.stem: Explain how adverse selection can cause market failure in insurance markets.
items.answer: Insurers cannot distinguish high-risk from low-risk customers, so they set an average premium. Low-risk customers find this too expensive and leave, raising the average risk and premiums, so the market shrinks or collapses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: asymmetric information; 1 mark: average premium drives out low-risk; 1 mark: market shrinks [3]

items.stem: In Calvania, private health insurers refuse to cover older people at affordable premiums. Analyse why this may be a market failure.
items.answer: Asymmetric information and adverse selection: insurers cannot assess individual risk and set high average premiums, low-risk people leave, so cover is under-provided; healthcare is also a merit good with positive externalities.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: asymmetric information; 1 mark: adverse selection chain; 1 mark: under-provision; 1 mark: merit good/externality [4]

items.stem: Distinguish between static efficiency and dynamic efficiency.
items.answer: Static efficiency (productive and allocative) is efficiency at a point in time with given technology; dynamic efficiency is the improvement in efficiency over time through innovation and investment.

(b) Static efficiency (productive and allocative) is efficiency at a point in time with given technology; dynamic efficiency is the improvement in efficiency over time through innovation and investment.

items.stem: The government of Korvia is reviewing whether markets for chocolate bars and for cement services are working efficiently. Discuss the extent to which perfect competition is the most efficient market structure.
items.answer: Arguments for: In LR perfect competition P = MC = min ATC, so firms are productively and allocatively efficient; no X-inefficiency. Arguments against / evaluation: No funds for R&D so little dynamic efficiency; no economies of scale; assumptions unrealistic; natural monopoly may have lower costs; efficiency must be weighed against equity. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Which market structure is often argued to promote dynamic efficiency?
options: A market with a price ceiling below cost
Monopoly or oligopoly earning long-run supernormal profit
A market with no barriers and no profit
items.answer: Monopoly or oligopoly earning long-run supernormal profit
items.markingKey: Supernormal profits can fund R&D (Schumpeter); competition may also spur innovation.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Distinguish between static efficiency and dynamic efficiency. (b) Explain the conditions needed for an economy to achieve Pareto optimality.
items.answer: (a) Static efficiency (productive and allocative) is efficiency at a point in time with given technology; dynamic efficiency is the improvement in efficiency over time through innovation and investment. (b) It must be productively efficient (on the PPC, firms at minimum cost) and allocatively efficient (P = MC in all markets), with no market failures.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: productive; 1 mark: allocative; 1 mark: P = MC everywhere/no market failure [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the conditions needed for an economy to achieve Pareto optimality. (b) Explain why a Pareto optimal allocation may still be considered unfair.
items.answer: (a) It must be productively efficient (on the PPC, firms at minimum cost) and allocatively efficient (P = MC in all markets), with no market failures. (b) Pareto optimality says nothing about distribution: an allocation where one person has almost everything can be Pareto optimal because any change would make them worse off.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: productive; 1 mark: allocative; 1 mark: P = MC everywhere/no market failure [3] (b) 1 mark: efficiency not equity; 1 mark: example [2]

items.stem: Lumen Ltd, a monopoly supplier of bus journeys in Esteria, spent $12 million on research. Over 2 years its average cost fell from $120 to $102 per unit while output stayed at 1 million units a year. Calculate (a) the percentage fall in average cost and (b) the annual cost saving. (c) Explain whether this is evidence of dynamic efficiency.
items.answer: (a) 15% (b) $18 million a year (c) Yes: costs fell over time through innovation funded by profit; the research cost is recovered in about 0.7 years of savings, though consumers gain only if lower costs are passed on in price or quality.
items.markingKey: (a) (120 − 102)/120 × 100 = 15% [1]; (b) 18 × 1m = $18m [1]; (c) definition of dynamic efficiency applied [1] + evaluative point (pass-through to consumers / monopoly) [1].

items.stem: The table shows the utility of two people under five allocations of resources (utility values). P: Leila 57, Priya 40; Q: Leila 56, Priya 40; R: Leila 57, Priya 46; S: Leila 64, Priya 42; T: Leila 66, Priya 37. Starting from allocation P, identify which moves are Pareto improvements and explain.
items.answer: Pareto improvements: R, S. In these moves neither person is worse off and at least one is better off; the other moves make someone worse off.
items.markingKey: For each allocation compare both utilities with P [2]; correct list [1]; reason: no-one worse off, someone better off [1].

items.stem: (a) Explain what is meant by a Pareto optimal allocation of resources. (b) ‘A Pareto optimal allocation of resources is the best outcome for society.’ Evaluate this statement.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Pareto optimum means no waste; any change would harm someone. (b) Case for the view: Pareto optimum means no waste; any change would harm someone. Case against / evaluation: Many Pareto optima exist, some very unequal; equity considerations; dynamic issues; value judgements needed. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: The free-rider problem arises because
options: consumers buy too much of demerit goods
people can benefit from a good without paying for it
firms charge prices above marginal cost
items.answer: people can benefit from a good without paying for it
items.markingKey: Non-excludability means no one has an incentive to pay, so private firms will not supply the good.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how monopoly power leads to market failure. (b) Explain the difference between a merit good and a public good.
items.answer: (a) A monopolist restricts output and raises price above MC, so P > MC (allocative inefficiency) and there is a deadweight welfare loss; it may also be X-inefficient. (b) A public good is non-rival and non-excludable and would not be provided at all by the market. A merit good is rival and excludable and is provided by the market, but in too small a quantity because its benefits are underestimated.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: higher price/lower output; 1 mark: P > MC; 1 mark: deadweight loss [3] (b) 1 mark each definition; 1 mark: not provided vs under-provided [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how monopoly power leads to market failure. (b) Explain how adverse selection can cause market failure in insurance markets.
items.answer: (a) A monopolist restricts output and raises price above MC, so P > MC (allocative inefficiency) and there is a deadweight welfare loss; it may also be X-inefficient. (b) Insurers cannot distinguish high-risk from low-risk customers, so they set an average premium. Low-risk customers find this too expensive and leave, raising the average risk and premiums, so the market shrinks or collapses.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: higher price/lower output; 1 mark: P > MC; 1 mark: deadweight loss [3] (b) 1 mark: asymmetric information; 1 mark: average premium drives out low-risk; 1 mark: market shrinks [3]

items.stem: A lighthouse on the coast of Istrana warns all passing ships. Which type of market failure is illustrated?
items.answer: Public good
items.markingKey: Public good: the market outcome is not allocatively efficient for this reason.

items.stem: Used-car sellers in Fendaria know about hidden faults that buyers cannot detect. Which type of market failure is illustrated?
items.answer: Asymmetric information
items.markingKey: Asymmetric information: the market outcome is not allocatively efficient for this reason.

items.stem: In Pelora, private markets supply too little education and too many sugary drinks. To what extent do you agree that government intervention is always needed when there is market failure?
items.answer: Arguments for: Public goods are not provided; externalities lead to over/under-production; information failure; monopoly; intervention can correct. Arguments against / evaluation: Government failure (information, incentives, cost of intervention); private solutions (Coase bargaining, reputation, warranties); size of failure matters. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
